full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. ANTONIO SARIO Y SERRANO AND MACARIO PEREZ, JR. Y MERCADO, ACCUSED; ANTONIO SARIO Y SERRANO, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > E. Title V – Crimes Relative to Opium and Other Prohibited Drugs > 1. Repealed. See instead Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165, Art. II, as amended by RA 10640; See also AM 18-03-16-SC)
topics: Chain of custody: the four links (Kamad)
Third link: non-presentation of the officer who received the drugs at the crime laboratory
Fourth link: stipulated chemist testimony silent on post-examination handling
Unsigned inventory and initials-only markings not fatal
Rule 122, Sec. 11(a): acquittal benefits a non-appealing co-accused who plea-bargained

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 1. Object or Real Evidence > c. Chain of Custody

doctrine:
In illegal sale and illegal possession of dangerous drugs (Secs. 5 and 11, RA 9165), the drug itself is the *corpus delicti*. The prosecution must prove its identity with moral certainty through an unbroken chain of custody covering the four links in *People v. Kamad*: (1) seizure and marking by the apprehending officer; (2) turnover to the investigating officer; (3) turnover to the forensic chemist; and (4) turnover by the forensic chemist to the court. Every person who handled the item must describe its condition and the precautions taken (*Mallillin v. People*). Reiterated.

**The third link is broken when the police officer who received the drugs at the crime laboratory is not presented**, leaving no evidence of the drugs' condition and safekeeping until the chemist retrieved them. **The fourth link is broken when the chemist's testimony is dispensed with by a stipulation covering only her qualifications, her receipt of the request and specimens, and the test results.** Such a stipulation says nothing on how the drugs were handled, stored and preserved after examination and before submission to the court (*People v. Supat*). These gaps create reasonable doubt and require acquittal. By contrast, the accused's failure to sign the inventory (when photographs show his presence) is inconsequential. So are markings that use only the accused's initials instead of the seizing officer's initials and the date, time and place required by the PNP Manual, as long as they segregate the items from other evidence.

**Under Rule 122, Section 11(a), a favorable judgment on appeal benefits a co-accused who did not appeal if it rests on a ground applicable to him. This holds even if he pleaded guilty to a lesser offense under a plea bargain and was convicted** (following *People v. Cordova*). A broken chain of custody that renders all the drugs presented in the cases unreliable, including those underlying the co-accused's charges, is such a ground.
facts:
On July 22, 2017, police officers conducted a buy-bust operation in Barangay San Antonio, Los Baños, Laguna. Introduced by an informant, poseur-buyer PO1 Estrada handed a marked PHP 500 bill to Macario Perez, Jr., who passed it to accused-appellant Antonio Sario. Sario took a sachet of shabu from his pocket and handed it to Perez, who gave it to PO1 Estrada. After the arrest, Sario produced two more sachets and the marked money from his pockets, and Perez produced one sachet. At the scene, PO1 Estrada marked the sachets "AS-BB," "AS1," "AS2" and "MP1," and inventoried and photographed them. This was done in the presence of the accused, a media representative and a barangay kagawad. The accused did not sign the inventory receipts but were given copies.

PO1 Estrada kept the items and prepared the requests at the station. He then personally brought them to the Regional Crime Laboratory, where PO3 Villela received them at 4:30 a.m. Forensic chemist PCINSP Huelgas found the specimens positive for shabu: 0.07 g (AS-BB), 5.52 g and 5.95 g (AS1 and AS2), and 0.04 g (MP1). Her testimony was dispensed with by a stipulation covering only her qualification, the receipt of the requests and specimens, her examination and reports, and her lack of personal knowledge of the seizure. PO3 Villela was not presented.

Sario was charged with illegal sale of 0.07 gram of shabu together with Perez (Crim. Case No. 30023-17-C) and with illegal possession of 11.47 grams (Crim. Case No. 30024-17-C). Perez was separately charged with illegal possession (Crim. Case No. 30025-17-C). During trial, Perez entered into plea bargaining and pleaded guilty to two counts of illegal possession of drug paraphernalia, which the RTC approved in a May 9, 2018 Order. Sario claimed frame-up.

On September 19, 2018, the RTC of Calamba City (Branch 36) convicted Sario on both charges and imposed life imprisonment and a fine for each. The CA affirmed on June 29, 2020. On appeal, Sario argued improper markings, the non-presentation of PO3 Villela, the inadequate stipulation on the chemist's testimony, the absence of an elected official at the inventory, and his unsigned inventory receipt.
issues: Whether the alleged lapses in the marking and inventory of the seized drugs, including the accused's unsigned inventory receipt, compromised their integrity.
Whether the prosecution established the third and fourth links of the chain of custody.
Whether Sario's acquittal benefits his co-accused Perez, who did not appeal and had pleaded guilty to a lesser offense.
ruling:
**1. No.** The Court held these arguments without merit, quoting with approval the CA's ruling. The inventory was made at the scene in the presence of Sario, a barangay kagawad and a media representative, and the photographs show their presence. It is not unusual for an accused to refuse to sign the inventory, and that refusal alone cannot exculpate him. The markings "AS-BB," "AS1" and "AS2," using Sario's initials, sufficiently separated the items from other evidence and prevented switching or contamination.

**2. No. The third and fourth links were not established, so Sario must be acquitted.** On the third link, PO1 Estrada delivered the drugs to the crime laboratory, where PO3 Villela received them, but PO3 Villela was never presented. As in *People v. Hernandez*, nothing on record shows the condition of the drugs or the precautions taken while they were in his custody until the chemist retrieved them. The Court "will not, as it cannot, speculate on such matters."

On the fourth link, the only evidence was PCINSP Huelgas's stipulated testimony. It covered only her qualification, the receipt of the requests and specimens, her positive findings, and her lack of personal knowledge of the seizure. It said nothing about the management, storage or preservation of the drugs after examination and before their submission to the court. As held in *People v. Supat*, such stipulations "do not prove how the drugs were handled." These gaps make it impossible to exclude contamination, substitution or alteration. **The *corpus delicti* was not proved with moral certainty.**

**3. Yes.** Rule 122, Section 11(a) allows a judgment on appeal by one accused to benefit those who did not appeal, if it is favorable and applicable to them. *People v. Cordova* applied this even to an accused who had pleaded guilty to, and been convicted of, a lesser offense. Sario's acquittal rests on gaps that render "defective and deficient all shabu presented by the prosecution in the cases a quo, including those related to the charges against Perez." Perez therefore benefits.
disposition: The appeal was GRANTED. The CA Decision of June 29, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 12743 was REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Sario was ACQUITTED in Criminal Case Nos. 30023-17-C and 30024-17-C and ordered released unless held for another lawful cause. The RTC's May 9, 2018 Order in Criminal Case Nos. 30023-17-C and 30025-17-C was SET ASIDE, and Perez was ACQUITTED in those cases on reasonable doubt and ordered released unless held for another lawful cause. The Director General of the Bureau of Corrections was directed to report the action taken within five days, and entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

bar_questions.q: In a buy-bust operation, PO2 Cruz seized a sachet of shabu from Andres. He marked it at the scene and inventoried and photographed it in the presence of Andres, a barangay councilor and a media representative. PO2 Cruz personally delivered the sachet to the crime laboratory, where PO1 Dela Paz received it. Forensic chemist Reyes later examined it and found it positive for shabu. At trial, PO1 Dela Paz was not presented. The parties stipulated only that Reyes is an expert, that she received the request and the specimen, that the specimen tested positive as stated in her report, and that she has no personal knowledge of the seizure. Andres was convicted of illegal sale. On appeal, he argues that the chain of custody was broken. Is he correct?

alac.answer: Yes. The third and fourth links of the chain of custody were not established, so Andres must be acquitted.
alac.legal_basis: In drug cases, the dangerous drug is the corpus delicti, and its identity must be proved with moral certainty through an unbroken chain of custody: seizure and marking, turnover to the investigating officer, turnover to the forensic chemist, and turnover by the chemist to the court (People v. Kamad). The non-presentation of the officer who received the drug at the laboratory breaks the third link. A stipulation on the chemist's testimony that does not cover how the drug was handled and preserved after examination breaks the fourth. (People v. Sario, G.R. No. 264409, April 13, 2026)
alac.application: No one testified on the condition of the sachet while it was in PO1 Dela Paz's custody, from his receipt until Reyes retrieved it, or on the precautions he took. The stipulation on Reyes's testimony covers only her qualifications, her receipt of the specimen and her results. It is silent on how the sachet was stored and preserved after examination until it reached the court. The court cannot fill these gaps by assumption, so substitution or contamination cannot be ruled out.
alac.conclusion: Andres must be acquitted because the identity of the corpus delicti was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

bar_questions.q: In another drug case, both the officer who received the specimen at the laboratory and the forensic chemist testified in detail on how it was received, sealed, examined, stored in the evidence vault and brought to court. Accused Bruno argues only that (a) he did not sign the inventory receipt, although photographs show that he and the required witnesses were present during the inventory; and (b) the sachet was marked only with his initials, "BV," instead of the seizing officer's initials and the date, time and place of seizure as the PNP drug manual requires. Should Bruno be acquitted?

alac.answer: No. These lapses do not affect the integrity of the seized drug.
alac.legal_basis: The accused's refusal or failure to sign the inventory cannot by itself exculpate him where photographs show his presence, and that of the required witnesses, during the inventory. Markings using the accused's initials suffice if they separate the seized item from all other similar evidence and prevent switching or contamination. In People v. Sario (G.R. No. 264409, April 13, 2026), the Court upheld the CA's rejection of these same arguments and acquitted only because the third and fourth links were missing.
alac.application: Every link here is accounted for by testimony on custody and handling, including the laboratory receiving officer and the chemist. The photographs show Bruno's presence at the inventory, so his unsigned receipt is immaterial. The marking "BV" distinguished the sachet from other evidence; departing from the PNP manual's marking format does not by itself cast doubt on the drug's identity.
alac.conclusion: Bruno's arguments do not warrant an acquittal.

bar_questions.q: Carlo and Dante were jointly charged with illegal sale of shabu, and Dante was separately charged with illegal possession, based on sachets seized in a single buy-bust operation. During trial, Dante entered into a plea bargain, pleaded guilty to illegal possession of drug paraphernalia, and was convicted. Carlo went to trial, was convicted, and appealed. The Supreme Court acquitted Carlo because the prosecution failed to prove the third and fourth links of the chain of custody for all the sachets seized. Dante did not appeal. Does Carlo's acquittal benefit Dante?

alac.answer: Yes. Dante should also be acquitted.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 122, Section 11(a) of the Rules of Court, a judgment on an appeal taken by one or more of several accused affects those who did not appeal insofar as it is favorable and applicable to them. The rule applies even to a co-accused who pleaded guilty to, and was convicted of, a lesser offense (People v. Cordova). (People v. Sario, G.R. No. 264409, April 13, 2026)
alac.application: Carlo's acquittal rests on the broken chain of custody for all the sachets seized in the operation, including those underlying the charges against Dante. That ground applies equally to Dante. His plea bargain and conviction for a lesser offense do not bar him from benefiting.
alac.conclusion: Dante's conviction should be set aside, and he should be acquitted on reasonable doubt.

notes: First Division. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred. Promulgated April 13, 2026, within the June 30, 2026 cutoff. Footnote 8 states that the exact text of the Information in Criminal Case No. 30025-17-C could not be found in the records. The Court rejected the Section 21 arguments (no elected official at the inventory; unsigned receipt) by adopting the CA's ruling, which noted that a barangay kagawad and a media representative witnessed the inventory. It gave no separate discussion.
